h1: Whisky sensory training for marketing teams
title: Whisky Sensory Training for Marketing | Craft Beer School
desc: How to run responsible whisky sensory training for marketing teams: the glass, the dilution, the vocabulary and how to turn tasting notes into briefs.
teaser: Marketing teams write about smoke, vanilla and dried fruit every day. Few have been taught to find them in a glass.
standfirst: A marketer who can nose a whisky writes better briefs, better copy and better questions for the blender. This guide shows how a sensory session for a marketing team works and how to keep it safe and opt-in.
sections: Why marketers need a trained nose

Whisky copy runs on flavour words: honey, orchard fruit, sherry, peat smoke, oak spice. When the person writing those words has never picked them out of a glass, the copy drifts towards whatever the last campaign said. The blender reads the brief and has to guess what marketing meant.

Sensory training closes that gap. It does not turn a brand manager into a blender. It gives the team a shared vocabulary with the liquid team and the confidence to say a new expression tastes nothing like the story on the label.

A sensory session at work is a training session, not a party. We set the rules before the first glass is poured.

  • Participation is opt-in and within company policy. Nobody is asked why they are not tasting.
  • Non-drinkers are welcome. Nosing alone teaches most of the skill. We also provide aroma references they can smell without any alcohol.
  • Spit cups for everyone, used freely. Professionals spit.
  • Small measures, water on every table and food afterwards.
  • Nobody drives home after tasting. Sessions run at the end of the day with cabs arranged, or are nosing only.

Our guide to responsible whisky drinking and pacing covers the same ground for home tastings.

Use a tulip shaped nosing glass with a narrow rim. It gathers the aroma and keeps the alcohol from overwhelming the nose. A standard tumbler throws most of the aroma away.

Whisky at bottling strength, usually 40 to 46% ABV, numbs the nose quickly. Professional sensory panels commonly reduce samples to around 20% ABV with still, low mineral water before nosing. That roughly means equal parts whisky and water for a 40% whisky. Cask strength samples at 55 to 60% need more water. At around 20% the alcohol stops masking the aroma and the fruit, cereal and wood notes come forward.

Pour about 15 ml per sample. Five samples at that size is enough for a 90 minute session, especially when most of it ends up in the spit cup.
A vocabulary that maps to the liquid

Flavour wheels for whisky group aromas into families that the production team recognises. A simple working set for a marketing team:

  • Cereal: malt, biscuit, porridge. From the grain and the new make spirit.
  • Fruity and floral: pear, apple, banana, blossom. Largely from esters made in fermentation.
  • Peaty: smoke, iodine, medicinal. From malt dried over peat fires.
  • Woody: vanilla, coconut, toast, spice. From oak casks, especially ex-bourbon American oak.
  • Winey: dried fruit, nuts, sherry. From sherry or wine casks.
  • Off notes: sulphury, feinty, cardboard. Worth knowing so nobody writes them up as complexity.

Our guide to using a whisky aroma wheel goes further.

A first session for a team of up to 20 runs well in this order.

  1. Aroma references (20 minutes). Jars of vanilla pod, dried apricot, green apple, cloves and a smoked ingredient. Everyone smells them before any whisky appears.
  2. A flight of four or five whiskies (45 minutes). Choose them to show contrast: a light blend, an ex-bourbon cask malt, a sherry cask malt, a peated malt. Include your own brand and one competitor.
  3. Write first, talk second. Each person notes three aromas before discussion. That stops the loudest voice setting everyone's notes.
  4. Brief writing (25 minutes). Teams rewrite a real tasting note or campaign line using what they found.
From tasting notes to better briefs

The output that matters is the brief. After a session, marketing teams tend to write briefs that name two or three specific target aromas instead of five vague adjectives. A blender can work with a brief that asks for more ex-bourbon vanilla and less sulphur. A brief that asks for a whisky that feels premium and modern gives them nothing to measure.

Training also changes how teams react to consumer research. When a panel calls a whisky harsh, a trained marketer asks whether that means alcohol heat, young spirit or a woody bitterness, because each has a different fix.

It works the other way too. A marketer who has nosed new make spirit next to a ten year old malt understands why aged stock is precious and why a blender cannot simply make more of a popular expression next quarter. That one comparison does more for sensible launch plans than any slide on maturation.

Before booking anything, do one small exercise with your team. Pick a single whisky from your own portfolio, dilute it to about 20% ABV, pour 15 ml each for those who opt in and ask everyone to write down three aromas before anyone speaks. Compare the lists with the official tasting note. The gap between the two is your training brief.
faqs: Do people have to drink whisky in a sensory session?
No. Sessions are opt-in, spit cups are provided and nosing alone teaches most of the skill. Non-drinkers can join using aroma references.
Why dilute whisky for sensory training?
At 40% ABV or more the alcohol numbs the nose. Reducing samples to around 20% ABV lets fruit, cereal and wood aromas come through.
How many whiskies should a first session include?
Four or five small samples of about 15 ml each, chosen for contrast, is plenty for a 90 minute session.
